faq.title: Are standard Telegram group chats and direct messages end-to-end encrypted?
faq.description: No. Standard Telegram private chats and group chats use client-to-server / server-to-client encryption. Messages are decrypted and stored on Telegram's distributed cloud infrastructure. Only Telegram 'Secret Chats' between two individual mobile devices are end-to-end encrypted where Telegram's servers cannot read the content.

faq.title: Can I use Telegram Secret Chats on Telegram Web or Desktop?
faq.description: No. Secret Chats are strictly device-specific and tied to the physical hardware security storage of your mobile smartphone. They do not sync to Telegram Desktop, Telegram Web, or secondary mobile devices because private encryption keys never leave the original device that initiated the chat.

faq.title: How do I visually verify that a Telegram Secret Chat is not intercepted by a Man-in-the-Middle?
faq.description: Open the Secret Chat, tap the user's profile avatar, and select 'Encryption Key'. Telegram displays a 12x12 visual pixel identicon and a 64-character hexadecimal fingerprint. Compare this image and code in person or over an out-of-band verified voice call; if both match identically, your session is cryptographically secure.

html:
Over 900 million active users rely on Telegram for daily communications, political activism, cryptocurrency communities, and personal conversations. A pervasive misconception among casual users is that Telegram is automatically "end-to-end encrypted like Signal or WhatsApp." In reality, Telegram's default architecture is a Cloud-Based Centralized Messaging Service. By default, your standard Telegram chats, groups, and media are decrypted and stored across Telegram's worldwide server clusters to enable multi-device synchronization and instant search.

For confidential, sensitive, or journalistic communication, users must manually initiate Telegram Secret Chats. Secret Chats utilize Telegram's custom cryptographic protocol, MTProto 2.0, enforcing genuine end-to-end encryption (E2EE) between two physical devices. Understanding the mathematical mechanics of MTProto 2.0, the differences between cloud chats and Secret Chats, and the steps required to verify cryptographic identicons is critical to maintaining digital privacy.

Cloud Chats vs. Secret Chats: The Fundamental Architectural Divide

Telegram operates two completely distinct messaging architectures within the same client application:

Architectural Attribute Standard Telegram Cloud Chats Telegram Secret Chats
Encryption Model Client-Server-Client (Server holds decryption keys) True End-to-End (E2EE) (Only devices hold keys)
Multi-Device Sync Instant sync across Phone, Desktop, Web, Tablet Zero sync; permanently locked to initiating device
Cloud Storage & Backups Stored on Telegram server clusters indefinitely Zero server storage; exists only in device RAM/sandbox
Self-Destruct Timers Auto-delete optional (metadata may persist) Cryptographic Ephemeral Deletion across both devices
Group Support Up to 200,000 members in supergroups 1-on-1 conversations only (no group Secret Chats)
Forwarding & Screenshots Freely forwardable; screenshots unrestricted Forwarding disabled; screenshot detection alerts triggered

MTProto 2.0 Cryptographic Protocol Mechanics

While industry peers (Signal, WhatsApp, Matrix) rely on the standardized Double Ratchet algorithm with Curve25519, Telegram engineers developed MTProto. Following academic scrutiny of MTProto 1.0, Telegram released MTProto 2.0, which fixed theoretical malleability flaws and authenticated-encryption vulnerabilities.

1. Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange over Ephemeral Channels

When User A initiates a Secret Chat with User B:

  1. User A's client generates a private random scalar \(a\) and calculates their public Diffie-Hellman value:

    \[g_a = g^a \pmod p\]

    where \(g\) is a fixed generator and \(p\) is a 2048-bit safe prime verified by the client.
  2. User A sends \(g_a\) to the Telegram server. Telegram forwards \(g_a\) to User B without learning private scalar \(a\).
  3. User B's client generates private scalar \(b\), calculates \(g_b = g^b \pmod p\), and computes the shared cryptographic master key:

    \[K = (g_a)^b \pmod p = g^{ab} \pmod p\]

  4. User B transmits \(g_b\) back to User A, who calculates \(K = (g_b)^a \pmod p\). Both devices now share an identical 2048-bit secret key \(K\). Because the server only saw \(g_a\) and \(g_b\), solving the Discrete Logarithm Problem to deduce \(K\) is computationally infeasible!

2. AES-256-IGE Symmetric Encryption

Once key \(K\) is established, messages are encrypted using AES-256 in Infinite Garble Extension (IGE) mode. In IGE mode, each plaintext block is XORed with the preceding plaintext block and preceding ciphertext block, propagating bit errors infinitely forward. MTProto 2.0 pairs AES-IGE with SHA-256 MAC authentication, ensuring complete ciphertext integrity and protecting against chosen-ciphertext attacks (IND-CCA2).

Out-of-Band Key Verification: Defeating Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) Attacks

The mathematical security of Diffie-Hellman hinges on a single condition: Did Telegram's server relay the authentic \(g_a\) and \(g_b\), or did the server inject its own keys in the middle?

To eliminate reliance on Telegram's server integrity, MTProto implements visual Identicon Fingerprint Verification:

  1. Both clients compute the SHA-256 hash of the shared master key: \( ext{Hash} = ext{SHA-256}(K)\).
  2. The first 128 bits of the hash are mapped to a 12x12 visual pixel grid (Identicon) consisting of 4 distinct colors and geometric patterns.
  3. The remaining bits are rendered as four hexadecimal words (or an emoji string).

Step-by-Step Verification Procedure: Tap the contact's name at the top of the Secret Chat and select Encryption Key. Compare the visual matrix and hexadecimal string with your contact—either by meeting in person, scanning a physical QR code, or reading the values over an end-to-end encrypted voice call. If every pixel and character matches identically, a Man-in-the-Middle attack is mathematically impossible.

Ephemeral Storage Forensics and Self-Destruct Timers

Secret Chats allow users to set Self-Destruct Timers ranging from 1 second to 1 week. The timer triggers only after the recipient opens and reads the message (marked by two green checkmarks).

When the timer expires, the Telegram client overwrites the local SQLite database sectors using cryptographic zero-wiping and deletes associated media caches from the app's sandboxed storage directory. However, forensic mobile investigators note several caveats:

  • Android Shared Storage Leaks: If third-party photo gallery apps or automatic cloud backup tools (Google Photos, OneDrive) have access to device storage, media files temporarily cached in app storage could theoretically be duplicated before self-destruction triggers. Ensure that Save to Gallery is explicitly disabled in Telegram settings.
  • RAM Cache Scraping: Unencrypted message fragments may remain in unallocated volatile RAM until the operating system reallocates that memory space. Powering off or restarting the device securely purges volatile memory.

Step-by-Step: Hardening Telegram for Maximum Privacy

To ensure your Telegram client leaves zero digital footprints, execute these configuration steps:

  1. Always Launch Secret Chats: Open a contact's profile, tap the three dots (⋮), and tap Start Secret Chat. Never discuss sensitive topics in standard blue cloud chats.
  2. Lock Down Phone Number Visibility: Go to Settings > Privacy and Security > Phone Number. Set Who can see my phone number to Nobody, and set Who can find me by my number to My Contacts.
  3. Disable Peer-to-Peer Calls: Navigate to Settings > Privacy and Security > Calls > Peer-to-Peer and select Never (or My Contacts). This forces voice calls to route through Telegram's proxy servers, preventing an adversary from discovering your home residential IP address via direct WebRTC packet inspection.
  4. Enable Local App Passcode Lock: Go to Settings > Privacy and Security > Passcode Lock. Enable an independent PIN or biometric lock. Telegram will encrypt the local database keys using SQLCipher, preventing anyone who physically picks up your unlocked phone from reading Secret Chats.

MTProto 2.0 vs. The Signal Protocol (Double Ratchet): Deep Cryptographic Comparison

To evaluate whether Telegram Secret Chats meet enterprise and journalistic threat models, cryptographers compare MTProto 2.0 with the globally recognized standard for end-to-end encryption: the Signal Protocol (utilized by Signal and WhatsApp):

  • Key Ratcheting Mechanics: The Signal Protocol continuously updates session keys using the Double Ratchet (combining a symmetric KDF ratchet with an asymmetric Diffie-Hellman ratchet). Every single individual message generates a fresh ephemeral key! If an attacker compromises a single session key, they cannot decrypt earlier messages (Forward Secrecy) nor subsequent messages (Future Secrecy / Post-Compromise Security). MTProto 2.0 in Secret Chats provides Forward Secrecy through periodic key rotation (every 100 messages or 1 week), but does not achieve per-message asymmetric ratcheting.
  • Cryptographic Primitives: Signal relies on standard modern elliptic curves (Curve25519) with HMAC-SHA256 and AES-256-GCM. MTProto 2.0 relies on custom 2048-bit finite field modular arithmetic, SHA-256 message keys, and AES-256-IGE. While modern cryptanalysis has confirmed MTProto 2.0's IND-CCA2 security, custom cryptographic constructions are generally scrutinized more heavily than established NIST/RFC standards.
  • Closed Server Infrastructure: Signal and Matrix open-source both client and server source code. While Telegram's mobile client applications are fully open-source (reproducible builds available on Android and iOS), Telegram's cloud server backend remains closed-source proprietary software.

Forensic RAM Extraction and Physical Device Vulnerabilities

Even with pristine end-to-end encryption over the air, physical access to an unlocked or seized smartphone presents profound forensic challenges:

  1. SQLCipher Database Encryption: When a user enables Telegram's Passcode Lock, the local client utilizes SQLCipher (or custom AES database encryption) with a key derived via PBKDF2 using thousands of iterations. Without the user's PIN or passphrase, raw database files on the flash storage cannot be mounted or queried by forensic tools like Cellebrite or GrayKey.
  2. Android Accessibility Service Exploits: Malicious surveillance spyware (such as Pegasus or commercial stalkerware) does not attempt to break MTProto's 2048-bit mathematics. Instead, it abuses Android's Accessibility Services or screen-recording APIs to scrape plaintext message text directly from the UI view hierarchy before encryption occurs, or after decryption is rendered on screen.
  3. Notification Previews and OS Logging: On default Android and iOS setups, incoming Secret Chat notifications may temporarily cache plaintext sender names or preview snippets inside system notification daemons. Users must configure Telegram to display "No details" on the lock screen.

Comprehensive Telegram Hardening Checklist for High-Risk Individuals

For journalists, political dissidents, and whistleblowers operating in hostile jurisdictions, execute this complete hardening workflow:

  • Enable Two-Step Verification with a strong, 20+ character master password and non-SMS recovery methods.
  • Set Auto-Delete Account to 1 month of inactivity under Settings > Privacy and Security > Delete My Account.
  • Disable Link Previews in Secret Chats to prevent Telegram servers from pre-fetching URLs and alerting webmasters to your IP address.
  • Configure Secret Chat Self-Destruct Timers to 30 seconds or less for all sensitive discussions.
  • Never allow Telegram access to your physical address book / contact synchronization.
  • Periodically inspect Settings > Devices and terminate any unrecognized or obsolete active login sessions immediately.
  • Use a dedicated VPN or SOCKS5 proxy to conceal your physical connection IP address from Telegram's transport servers.
